title: Keep Ronnie Coleman's name out of your unworthy hardgainer's mouth
summary: NH rants against non-lifters who mock Ronnie Coleman's current condition and use it to claim heavy lifting is harmful. He argues Coleman's decline came from refusing to heal injuries, training straight after surgeries, and a family genetic predisposition to hip problems, not from heavy weights, and calls on the iron community to defend lifting against this propaganda.
claims: Ronnie Coleman's heavy lifting videos (800 lb squat, 'light weight baby') capture the primal energy of fighting a heavy weight and are an integral part of lifting culture
Heavy is relative: any weight that challenges you and makes you channel something animalistic counts
Before he started squatting he watched Coleman's 800 lb squat clip for inspiration; pro bodybuilders inspired much of his early lifting
Pro bodybuilders can serve as inspiration for beginners; the problem starts when you get emotionally attached to them
Non-lifters who mock Coleman's state are really attacking lifting itself and are motivated by jealousy and insecurity
There are two types of men: those motivated by seeing someone get after it, and those who mock it to avoid having to work
The mainstream idea that heavy lifting is bad prevents people reaching their best; heavy lifting is key for strength and for natural and enhanced lifters
Coleman genuinely trained extremely hard while on drugs, unlike many who barely train and still get huge
Coleman's body was not wrecked by heavy lifting but by refusing to let injuries heal and training right after surgeries
Pushing the limits will sometimes injure you; that is acceptable as long as you recover properly
Many pro bodybuilders do not care about their health because they chase perfection and are willing to die for it; he respects that if they do not complain later
Resistance training is the best way to prevent deterioration of the spine and joints, but taken too far it produces the opposite
Coleman had a genetic predisposition: his grandfather and father, who never lifted, both needed hip replacements
There is a history of leg paralysis in his family, but that will not stop him training his legs while they work
When Coleman dies, mockers will blame heavy lifting rather than PED use, which is the real issue
Lifters must defend their practices and share their truths against outsiders and traitors inside the community spreading anti-heavy-lifting lies
